transcript.text: But I cannot get a job.

transcript.speaker: Th
transcript.text: That is not true. You can get a job, but it is impossible to get the job you wanted, an executive secretary position. And how hard that is! This fantasy was so beautiful. And how hard it is to let go of that beautiful picture you had in your mind.

transcript.speaker: Pt
transcript.text: It was a very beautiful picture.

metadata.start_state_desc: Patient uses the defense of 'hopelessness' to avoid the pain of reality.
metadata.end_state_desc: Patient drops the defense and connects with the genuine grief of the lost fantasy.

training_value.pedagogical_shape: Grief Opening Sequence: Transitioning from 'hopelessness' (defense) to 'grief' (feeling) by validating the beauty of the lost fantasy.
what_model_should_learn: How to distinguish 'hopelessness' (a defense against feeling) from 'grief' (the healing feeling).
How to validate the emotional weight of a fantasy ('It was a very beautiful picture') to allow the patient to let it go.
How to use gentle reality testing to puncture denial without being punitive.

source_location.section: Vignette Three: Hopelessness When Denial Breaks Down

transcript.speaker: Pt
transcript.text: I was getting a glass of water at the sink... All I know is I blew up, turned around, and threw a glass of water in her face. She got all pissed off and told me to get the hell out...

transcript.speaker: Th
transcript.text: It sounds like you were not feeling too good about having sex with the woman at the bar. What was that feeling?

transcript.speaker: Pt
transcript.text: I felt guilty.

transcript.speaker: Th
transcript.text: You felt guilty for having sex with this other woman, but the way you dealt with the guilt was to go home and provoke your wife to punish you, even though she didn’t know the real reason.

transcript.speaker: Pt
transcript.text: I hadn’t thought of that. I was just angry with her for being hard on me.

transcript.speaker: Th
transcript.text: You thought she was being hard on you. Yet by throwing the water on her for no reason, you were hard on her, and you invited her to punish you. You felt guilty, but rather than face your guilt, you goaded her into punishing you.

transcript.speaker: Pt
transcript.text: That’s true. I didn’t feel right about it afterward.

metadata.start_state_desc: Patient acts out ragefully (throwing water) and feels victimized by wife's reaction.
metadata.end_state_desc: Patient understands the behavior was a mechanism to provoke punishment for his own hidden guilt.

training_value.pedagogical_shape: Causal Mapping of Provocation: Linking the feeling (Guilt) to the Defense (Provoking Punishment).
what_model_should_learn: How to interpret 'Provocation' as a defense against bearing internal guilt (RM_02).
How to explain that patients 'invite' external punishment to relieve internal pressure (RM_05).

transcript.speaker: Th
transcript.text: What is the feeling toward him for taking your girlfriend?

transcript.speaker: Pt
transcript.text: I feel like I could explode! [Yells.]

transcript.speaker: Th
transcript.text: And what is that feeling?

transcript.speaker: Pt
transcript.text: Rage.

transcript.speaker: Th
transcript.text: How do you experience that rage in your body?

transcript.speaker: Pt
transcript.text: [Begins punching with his fists and stomping the floor.]

transcript.speaker: Th
transcript.text: I see that’s what you want to do. You want to get this rage out of you by moving rather than to let yourself feel it inside. If you don’t shake this feeling out of your body, could you let your feet stay still on the floor, and leave your arms on the armrest? How do you experience this rage in your body now?

metadata.start_state_desc: Impulsive patient acts out (stomping/punching) to discharge tension.
metadata.end_state_desc: Therapist blocks the discharge to force internal experience of the rage.

training_value.pedagogical_shape: Blocking 'Discharge' to build 'Affect Tolerance'.
what_model_should_learn: How to differentiate 'Acting Out' (movement) from 'Feeling' (internal sensation).
How to physically constrain a patient (verbally) to force anxiety regulation and deepening.

source_location.section: Skipping the Step of Experiencing the Feeling in the Body

transcript.speaker: The Buddha
transcript.text: Kaccana, this world is mostly bound by clinging, taking hold of something or other.

transcript.speaker: Kaccanagotta
transcript.text: What is the view that abandons clinging?

transcript.speaker: The Buddha
transcript.text: When one sees dependent origination as it is—‘When this exists, that comes to be; with the arising of this, that arises’—one does not cling to any view of existence or non-existence.

transcript.speaker: Kaccanagotta
transcript.text: So right view is seeing conditions?

transcript.speaker: The Buddha
transcript.text: Just so. Seeing conditional arising and conditional cessation.

transcript.speaker: Kaccanagotta
transcript.text: This seems a middle way beyond views.

transcript.speaker: The Buddha
transcript.text: It is the middle by which the Tathāgata teaches the Dhamma.

metadata.start_state_desc: Student asks how to avoid clinging.
metadata.end_state_desc: Buddha replaces the binary with the causal algorithm of dependent origination.

training_value.pedagogical_shape: Replace Broken Framework → Causal Model
what_model_should_learn: After unmaking a view, supply a clean replacement model.
Dependent origination = core Buddhist causal logic.
Teach by simple repetition: ‘When this exists, that arises.’

transcript.speaker: Dighanakha
transcript.text: Master Gotama, this is my view: ‘I take no view. Nothing is acceptable to me.’

transcript.speaker: The Buddha
transcript.text: Aggivessana, do you hold that view as true?

transcript.speaker: Dighanakha
transcript.text: Yes, Master Gotama, this is truly my view.

transcript.speaker: The Buddha
transcript.text: But if you take that as true, then at least this one view is acceptable to you.

transcript.speaker: Dighanakha
transcript.text: Master Gotama, it seems this view does not stand as I thought.

transcript.speaker: The Buddha
transcript.text: When one says ‘Nothing is acceptable to me,’ that itself is something accepted.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: And Dighanakha’s view was thereby shaken.

metadata.start_state_desc: Dighanakha asserts a sweeping nihilistic doctrine.
metadata.end_state_desc: He is forced to see the self-contradiction in his universal negation.

training_value.pedagogical_shape: Self-Refutation Unmaking
what_model_should_learn: Expose contradictions by simply reflecting the student’s view back.
Universal negations (‘nothing is true’, ‘no view is valid’) collapse instantly.
UNMAKING can be gentle and precise, not aggressive.
